Article Title: China’s ecoonomy picks up pace with 4.5% growth in Q3
Article Text: BEIJING: China’s economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter of 2026, fuelled by global demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, which helped it offset weak domestic consumption and a deepening property market crisis. It is a recovery of sorts for the world’s second-largest economy as the growth fell to 4.3% in the second quarter, its lowest since 2022, weighed down by stagnant domestic demand and higher energy costs linked to the Iran war, offsetting the robust export growth.The economy generated about $16 trillion in output during the Jan-Sept period, according to data released by National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on Monday. However, the recovery remains uneven, with manufacturing and exports driving growth while household spending and investment continue to struggle, raising questions about the sustainability of the expansion. “The steady economic performance from the first three quarters has laid a good foundation for the achievement of the annual target,” Mao Shengyong, deputy director of NBS, said.
Article Summary: China's economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter of 2026, fuelled by global demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. The recovery remains uneven, with manufacturing and exports driving growth while household spending and investment continue to struggle.

Article Title: Russia ships 20 million barrels of oil to Asia via Arctic route amid shipping disruptions: Report
Article Text:
Russia's Arctic oil shipments exceeded 2025's full-season total of 13 million barrels, with another 5-10 million barrels expected by the end of the current navigation period

Gazprom Neft

plans to increase Arctic shipments

Russia has shipped nearly 20 million barrels of oil to Asia through the Northern Sea Route (NSR) since the start of the navigation season in July, almost 50 per cent more than during the corresponding period last year, as disruptions to traditional shipping corridors make the Arctic route more attractive, traders said and data showed.The volume shipped through the route by mid-October has already exceeded the 13 million barrels exported during the entire 2025 navigation season. Shipments could rise by another 5-10 million barrels before the current navigation period ends, according to preliminary estimates by traders, cited by Reuters.The NSR connects Russia's western ports with Asian markets through Arctic waters. Although the route is more hazardous and expensive to navigate, requiring icebreaker assistance, disruptions involving the Suez Canal, the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea have improved its appeal this year.Rising tanker freight rates, fuelled by the wars involving Iran and Ukraine, have added to the pressure on shipping costs. With conventional routes facing security risks and supply disruptions, Asian refiners have been looking for alternative sources of crude oil, making the higher cost of Arctic shipping more competitive against longer or riskier alternatives, traders said.For Moscow, the route also offers a strategic alternative to European waters, where tankers carrying Russian oil have faced repeated seizures this year.The expansion of Arctic shipments comes as Russian crude supplies to India face tighter availability and growing competition from China.Meanwhile, India remained the world's largest destination for Russian crude oil in September, although imports fell nearly 29 per cent from July levels as Chinese refiners stepped up purchases and tightened the availability of Russian supplies, according to ship-tracking data from Kpler.The report noted that Arctic shipments offer a more direct and potentially economical route to northern China during the navigation season. This could intensify competition between Chinese and Indian refiners for Russian crude, particularly as shipping costs and tighter supplies reduce the price advantage India previously enjoyed.India has relied heavily on Russian crude since 2022, when Moscow redirected oil exports away from Europe. However, the changing economics of Russian oil have prompted Indian refiners to consider alternatives, including supplies from the Middle East and Latin America.Gazprom Neft, one of Russia's major oil producers, plans to increase shipments through the NSR by around 35% this year compared with 2025, its chief executive Alexander Dyukov told journalists in Moscow on Friday.The route is also being used to transport liquefied natural gas (LNG) and other goods to Asian markets. LNG shipments are expected to increase this year following the launch of deliveries from the Arctic LNG project.Russia is seeking to expand the route's role in its trade with Asia. President Vladimir Putin said at an economic forum in Vladivostok in September that the country expects annual cargo turnover through the NSR to double to 70 million metric tonnes by the end of the decade.The increase in oil traffic is also being supported by Vostok Oil, Rosneft's major oil project in northern Russia, which began operations last month and is already contributing to rising volumes along the route.
Article Summary: Russia has shipped nearly 20 million barrels of oil to Asia through the Northern Sea Route (NSR) since the start of the navigation season in July. Shipments could rise by another 5-10 million barrels before the current navigation period ends. The expansion of Arctic shipments comes as Russian crude supplies to India face tighter availability.

Article Title: 'One SpaceX share for every kid in America': Can Elon Musk actually do it?
Article Text:
Musk's statement sets out a promise rather than a confirmed distribution plan. Until the eligibility rules, legal arrangements and method of transfer are made clear, it remains uncertain how the proposed giveaway would work in practice.

How many shares would Musk need?

Musk could transfer shares he already owns to eligible children.

SpaceX could issue additional shares as part of a new arrangement.

Musk's private shares could face restrictions

The legal and practical hurdles

Musk's hint at plan to deliver SpaceX share promise

Is Musk's promise feasible?

Who would qualify.

How the shares would be distributed.

Whether the company's rules permit the transfers.

How ownership by minors would be handled.

Elon Musk has said he will give every child in America one share of SpaceX in 2027. While the statement itself seems inchoate, it also raises questions about whether the ambitious promise can be fulfilled.The SpaceX CEO said the move would be the first of many such initiatives. However, turning the announcement into reality could prove complicated, given SpaceX's status as a privately held company and the legal and practical challenges of distributing shares to millions of children."Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk said in his announcement on his own platform, X.However, if Musk means every child under 18 living in the United States, the country has roughly 73 million children, based on recent US population estimates. This means he would have to distribute around 73 million shares, although the final number would depend on the eligibility criteria.There are two broad ways this could happen.The two options would have different implications for the company and its existing shareholders.The scale of the exercise would also raise questions about eligibility.It is not yet clear whether the promise would cover every person under 18, only US citizens, or children who meet other conditions. Those details would be essential to determining the number of shares required.Another key hurdle is that Musk's SpaceX shares are privately held. This means its shares cannot be transferred as easily as they are bought and sold.His private shares can be subject to restrictions on transfers. Musk could therefore face limits on how he distributes his holdings, depending on SpaceX's corporate rules and the terms governing its shares. Any large-scale transfer would need to account for those conditions.Giving shares to millions of children would involve more than transferring ownership. The plan would need to comply with applicable securities laws and SpaceX's corporate rules. The company may also need to address how such a large number of new shareholders would affect its ownership structure and administrative arrangements.The recipients' ages would add another layer of complexity.Since many beneficiaries would be minors, arrangements may be needed for adults or custodians to hold or manage their shares until the children are legally able to do so. The process would also require a reliable way to establish who qualifies, verify their details and transfer the shares to the right recipients.Tax implications could be another consideration for both the person making the gift and those receiving it.The treatment would depend on the structure of the giveaway and the rules that apply. With millions of potential recipients, even routine administrative steps could become a substantial undertaking.Elon Musk's response to Anthropic's announcement of committing the company's funds for public benefit does give a potential clue as to how he plans to fulfil his promise.Musk had suggested that he would distribute company shares directly to the public, rather than through a separate fund.He made the remarks in response to Anthropic's announcement to initially commit 5% of its shares to a public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation rises."I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," Musk wrote on X, "This is what I will be doing."Musk's comments suggest that he favours direct distribution over an intermediary fund. But giving a SpaceX share to millions of children would still involve significant legal and logistical hurdles.The idea is not necessarily impossible. A transfer of existing shares or a specially structured distribution could, in principle, provide a way to give children an ownership stake in SpaceX. But the scale of the proposal makes its execution far more complicated than an ordinary gift.There are various factors yet unannounced by Musk or SpaceX that would determine how the promise of US children having shares in the company plays out. It includes:For now, Musk's statement sets out a promise rather than a confirmed distribution plan. Until the eligibility rules, legal arrangements and method of transfer are made clear, it remains uncertain how the proposed giveaway would work in practice.
Article Summary: Elon Musk has said he will give every child in America one share of SpaceX in 2027. The SpaceX CEO said the move would be the first of many such initiatives. But turning the announcement into reality could prove complicated, given SpaceX's status as a privately held company and the legal and practical challenges of distributing shares.

Article Title: Asian shares are mixed with tech stocks volatile, and oil falls on Trump's Russian sanctions waiver
Article Text:
Asian shares remain mixed

Asian shares were mixed Monday as volatility in technology stocks persisted, while U.S. equity futures edged higher ahead of another week of American corporate earnings results.Oil prices fell more than 2% after U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sweeping sanctions on Russia, including on Russian energy.A sell-off of technology shares from Asia to Wall Street recently put downward pressure on stock markets, as investor concerns grow over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom.South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index was up 1.8% to 5,768.01 on Monday, after falling sharply last week. The Kospi is down more than 17% over the past month, and still well below the 9,000 mark it crossed in June at its peak on the global AI frenzy.Samsung Electronics was up 1.2%, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix added 0.4%.Japan’s Nikkei 225 lost 0.6% to 64,916.70. Japanese chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron fell 2.6%, and OpenAI investor SoftBank Group dropped 2%.“We’ve been arguing for a while that volatility in tech stocks would pick up as the AI bubble continued to inflate: sharp and short-lived sell-offs were common as the ‘dotcom’ bubble inflated, for example, even as the market ultimately made very large gains on net,” Capital Economics Head of Markets for Asia Pacific Thomas Mathews wrote in a commentary Monday.Hong Kong’s stock market was closed because of a holiday. The Shanghai Composite index edged 0.4% higher to 3,730.92, after China reported better-than-expected growth of 4.5% for its economy in the July-September quarter.CXMT, China’s leading memory chipmaker, fell more than 7% despite the company forecasting a strong profit for the first nine months.Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 was 0.4% higher at 8,845.70.Taiwan’s Taiex fell 0.6%. India’s Sensex slipped 0.9%.Indonesia’s benchmark stock index fell over 5% at its peak, to its lowest level since 2020, after it plunged over 11% on Friday following a warning from index provider MSCI that it would downgrade the country from its “emerging market” status.On Friday, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 declined 1.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3%, and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite sank 2.1%.Investors this week are watching for more big corporate earnings results from the U.S., including Meta, Netflix, General Motors, Tesla and IBM. Strong company earnings have been one factor that’s been keeping U.S. stocks robust lately.As technology shares face rising uncertainties, experts say government bonds might stand to benefit as investors look for relatively safe assets, though the bond market had also been turbulent over the past few weeks.The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury eased to around 5.07% early Monday, compared with roughly 5.13% Friday. It had hit 5.35% earlier this month at its highest level since 2002, as inflation worries from the Iran war-driven energy shock and growing U.S. government debt pushed yields higher — investors demanded more in return because of the additional risks.Oil prices were down early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, falling 2.5% to $107.16 per barrel.Benchmark U.S. crude dropped 2.2% to $96.84 per barrel.Oil fell after Trump late Friday signed an executive order to put new broad U.S. sanctions against Russia on hold just days before they were to come into effect, drawing disappointment from Ukraine, with the move likely resulting in more energy exports from Russia.Trump's decision came not long after he said earlier this month he had reached a diesel deal with Russia in an attempt to bring down elevated U.S. fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.But even with the decline, oil prices have remained elevated compared with those seen before the Iran war. Global oil supply risks are still high amid tensions in the Middle East, including uncertainty surrounding oil transport in the Strait of Hormuz, adding upward pressure to prices.The U.S. dollar fell to 157.98 Japanese yen from 158.10 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1218, down from $1.1234.
Article Summary: South Korea's benchmark Kospi index was up 1.8% to 5,768.01 on Monday, after falling sharply last week. China's Shanghai Composite index edged 0.4% higher to 3,730.92, after China reported better-than-expected growth of 4.5% for its economy in the July-September quarter. Oil prices fell more than 2% after U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sweeping sanctions on Russia.

Article Title: Oil prices ease as Trump waives Russia sanctions, Middle East risks persist
Article Text:
Crude prices ease below $110 per barrel

Oil prices fell on Monday as US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions and tariffs on Russia raised the prospect of additional fuel supplies entering the market. However, continuing security threats in the Middle East and uncertainty over US-Iran negotiations kept the outlook for crude volatile.Brent crude declined $1.56, or 1.42%, to $108.3, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was down 0.25, or 0.25%, at $101.2 a barrel.The previous week, US President Donald Trump had signed an executive order granting a waiver on key sanctions and tariffs imposed under the law known as the Graham Act. The legislation was signed last month after lawmakers urged the president to put pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.Secretary of state Marco Rubio said Trump would use up to 60 days to evaluate the economic consequences of the waiver.The move came after Trump reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to export diesel to the US. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy criticised the US actions, saying they would hurt Ukraine.Brent crude had climbed to $110 a barrel briefly on Friday, marking its first such level since May, as mounting tensions in the Middle East heightened concerns about the security of shipping routes and the availability of global energy supplies.The pressure on supplies has been compounded by attacks on commercial vessels. Gulf crude flows fell to approximately 8.5 million barrels per day on a seven-day average last week, down from more than 20 million barrels per day in the previous week, according to analytics firm Kpler. In a note issued on Friday, the firm also reported at least 10 confirmed incidents involving commercial vessels during the week.The risk of a wider regional confrontation remained in focus, with Egypt stating that it was prepared to offer Saudi Arabia the support required to protect its security and stability against Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.Despite Monday’s decline, crude markets face another week of potential price swings. Supply concerns across West Asia and stalled negotiations between the US and Iran are fuelling fears of further disruptions, while measures aimed at easing shortages are providing some relief, analysts said.Market participants will look to upcoming inventory figures for a clearer picture of supply and demand. The data under scrutiny include weekly crude stock estimates from the American Petroleum Institute (API), inventories at Cushing, total US oil stocks and crude imports.Developments around the Strait of Hormuz will also remain crucial to the market outlook. Any interruption to shipments through the strategic waterway could further restrict global oil supplies, adding to the uncertainty surrounding prices.
Article Summary: Brent crude declined $1.56, or 1.42%, to $108.3 a barrel on Monday. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was down 0.25, or 0. 25%, at $101.2 a barrel. US President Donald Trump had signed an executive order granting a waiver on key sanctions and tariffs imposed under the Graham Act.

Article Title: Venezuela signs 61 oil agreements, expects $76 billion in investments over five years
Article Text:
Venezuela signs 61 oil agreements

Venezuela expects to attract nearly $76 billion in oil investments over the next five years under recently signed agreements, acting President Delcy Rodriguez said on Saturday. A bilateral accord with the United States includes plans to drill 250 rigs and covers 17 oilfields, forming part of a broader package of 61 agreements signed by the two sides.Rodriguez said the proposed investments would deliver direct gains for Venezuela while also benefiting its partners."Major investments are coming," she said. "We are talking about investment of almost $76 billion over five years. Those investments will translate into direct benefits for our country in a win-win partnership, because our partner will also benefit."The agreements come as Venezuela opens up its energy sector to overseas investors following the removal of President Nicolas Maduro in January. The process has the backing of US President Donald Trump's administration.The proposed investments could help lift oil production in a country that holds the world's largest proven crude oil reserves but is producing far less than it did a decade ago.Rodriguez also cited rising output in Zulia, a western Venezuelan state, where production has climbed from 70,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 370,000 bpd.She expects output to reach 400,000 bpd by the end of this year, although she did not specify when the increase from 70,000 bpd began.The country's oil sector has struggled with prolonged underinvestment, operational difficulties at state-owned oil company PDVSA and US sanctions targeting the energy industry.Meanwhile, Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared in a US court earlier this week as they prepared to respond to an expanded indictment accusing them of conspiring to torture political opponents.The new charges, brought last Thursday, broaden the criminal case against the former Venezuelan president, 63, and Flores, 70. Both had earlier pleaded not guilty to allegations that they abused their positions to help drug traffickers transport cocaine. Their lawyers have also said they deny the torture allegations.The couple were captured by the US military in a raid ordered by Trump in January and subsequently flown to New York.
Article Summary: Venezuela expects to attract nearly $76 billion in oil investments over the next five years. A bilateral accord with the United States includes plans to drill 250 rigs and cover 17 oilfields. The proposed investments could help lift oil production in a country that holds world's largest proven crude oil reserves.

Article Title: Russia sanctions waiver buys time for India but offers no lasting certainty: GTRI
Article Text:
For now, it's a temporary waiver and not a long-lasting relief (Representative image)

Why did the US waive the tariffs?

US President Donald Trump's decision to waive additional tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil has provided temporary relief to India, but the pressure remains as the possibility of Washington restoring the duties is still there according to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI).The think tank said on Saturday that while the move eases the immediate threat of fresh trade penalties, the underlying legislation remains in force, allowing the US administration to withdraw the waiver and revive tariff pressure during future trade negotiations."For India, the waiver buys time but offers no lasting certainty. India should protect its energy security, buy oil on commercial terms and prepare for renewed US pressure. Temporary tariff relief is no basis for permanent trade concessions," GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava said, as quoted by PTI.Trump on Friday signed an executive order implementing the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, while simultaneously suspending certain sanctions and additional duties under the legislation.The law provides for additional tariffs of 100 per cent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas making fresh purchases from October 18.It also sets out a 500 per cent tariff increase on Russian goods. However, Trump invoked Section 115 of the legislation to waive the duties, citing US national interests."Pursuant to section 115(a) of the Graham Act, I hereby waive the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Graham Act or this order," the executive order stated.The waiver has no fixed expiry date and can be withdrawn. Existing Russia-related sanctions imposed under other executive orders remain unaffected.GTRI claimed several factors that may have influenced Washington's decision, including its domestic energy requirements, trade arrangements with China and ongoing negotiations with India.According to the think tank, the US agreed on October 9 to purchase Russian diesel to address domestic fuel shortages and elevated prices, making it difficult to justify penalties on other countries for similar purchases. "Punishing other countries for buying Russian energy while doing so itself would invite accusations of double standards," Srivastava said.The report also pointed to Washington's agreement not to raise tariffs on China until January 10, suggesting that imposing additional duties on India alone could complicate bilateral trade negotiations.GTRI noted that Russia's share of India's oil imports declined from 51 per cent in July to 44 per cent in August as Indian refiners increased purchases from the US and the UAE.In the meantime, despite the waiver, the US Trade Representative will continue monitoring Russian energy purchases, leaving Washington with the option of reviewing the relief.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump waived additional tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil. The move eases the immediate threat of fresh trade penalties, but the underlying legislation remains in force. The possibility of Washington restoring the duties is still there according to the Global Trade Research Initiative.

Article Title: Crude oil prices may fall to $80 in 2027: What could bring prices down?
Article Text:
Oil prices might ease by 2026 end

Middle East exports recover, but risks remain

Weak consumption weighs on the outlook

The global oil market could move from a supply crunch towards a surplus by the end of 2026, paving the way for lower crude prices next year, Goldman Sachs Research has said.The firm expects Brent crude to average $80 per barrel in 2027, provided supplies from the Middle East continue to recover and demand gradually improves.The forecast comes even as oil prices remain under pressure from the risk of further escalation in the US-Israel-Iran conflict. Goldman Sachs warned that renewed hostilities could prolong supply disruptions and delay the expected moderation in prices.Daan Struyven, co-head of global commodities research and head of oil research at Goldman Sachs, said the firm now expects Brent crude to reach $90 per barrel in December 2026. This is higher than its earlier projection of $85 per barrel. For 2027, however, the bank expects prices to average $80 per barrel.The changing outlook follows a sharp reduction in the gap between global oil demand and supply. In March, demand outstripped supply by 7.2 million barrels per day (mb/d). By September, the shortfall had narrowed to just 0.3 mb/d.Goldman Sachs attributed the improvement to three factors: the recovery in Middle Eastern oil exports, increased production outside the Persian Gulf and weaker consumption.Based on these trends, the bank expects supply to exceed demand in the fourth quarter of 2026, with the surplus continuing into 2027.Oil shipments from the Persian Gulf have shown signs of recovery despite the conflict. Goldman Sachs estimated that exports from the region had returned to around their 2025 average by late September, as exporters adapted to the situation and expanded transportation capacity.However, the improvement in supply has not eliminated concerns about further disruptions. Physical Brent prices for near-term delivery have risen above $130 per barrel, while benchmark Brent futures have recently traded above $100."Physical prices remain elevated because escalation threatens supply while near-record-low global inventories fuel strong restocking demand," Struyven said, as cited by ANI.Goldman Sachs estimates that the possibility of further disruptions is adding nearly $25 per barrel to crude prices in the form of a risk premium. The premium also reflects the prospect of additional inventory drawdowns if the conflict intensifies.Demand has also played a significant role in easing pressure on the global oil market. Consumption in the third quarter of 2026 was 3.3 mb/d lower than in the corresponding period a year earlier. China, the Middle East and developed Asian economies accounted for much of the weakness.The bank expects consumption to recover gradually as refined oil products become more available and affordable. Nevertheless, it does not expect demand to return fully to the level it might have reached in the absence of the conflict-related shock.In the fourth quarter of 2027, global oil demand is projected to remain 0.7 mb/d below that hypothetical trajectory. Goldman Sachs attributed part of the gap to faster adoption of electric vehicles and changes in fuel consumption patterns in China.The outlook for oil prices will therefore hinge on how quickly production and exports recover, how demand normalises and whether the conflict in the Middle East escalates again. While the anticipated supply surplus supports the bank's forecast of lower prices in 2027, renewed disruptions could keep crude elevated for longer than expected.
Article Summary: Goldman Sachs Research says global oil market could move from a supply crunch towards a surplus by the end of 2026. Firm expects Brent crude to average $80 per barrel in 2027, provided supplies from the Middle East continue to recover and demand gradually improves.

Article Title: Morgan Stanley sees risk asset bull market regaining momentum as growth, AI support returns
Article Text:
Bull market may regain momentum

Oil supply shock remains a key risk

US equities preferred, India faces challenges

Global markets could see risk assets regain momentum as strong economic growth, rising corporate earnings and AI-led productivity support returns despite higher bond yields, according to a Morgan Stanley report.The firm now favours global stocks over bonds, saying rising bond yields reflect a strong economy rather than a worsening economic situation.“As the forces driving yields higher begin to fade, we expect the bull market in risk assets to reassert itself,” the report said.Morgan Stanley said stronger economic growth continues to underpin corporate earnings, cash flows, employment, consumption and credit quality. Meanwhile, the adoption of and investment in artificial intelligence (AI) remain key drivers of productivity gains and business expansion.Global economic activity has remained firm despite higher energy prices and interest rates, with services and manufacturing activity showing signs of acceleration, the report noted.Productivity gains could also help wages and output grow without a corresponding increase in labour costs, potentially helping contain inflationary pressures.Despite its constructive outlook, Morgan Stanley cautioned that geopolitical tensions, energy supply disruptions and persistent inflation could threaten the market's momentum.The report identified an oil supply shock that forces central banks to tighten monetary policy excessively as a key risk to its positive outlook for risk assets.“If inflation becomes uncontained, central banks must move from removing accommodation to actively destroying demand,” the report said.It also warned that refined oil products, particularly diesel, remain vulnerable to supply disruptions. Any such disruption could push energy costs higher and feed into inflation.While the firm expects economic growth to remain supportive of risk assets, a sustained energy shock could change its outlook.Within equities, Morgan Stanley maintained its overweight position on US markets, citing resilient economic growth, strong corporate earnings and continued AI adoption.The firm remained cautious on European equities because of energy-related headwinds, although it identified opportunities in the banking and utilities sectors.Indian equities, meanwhile, face challenges from comparatively weaker forward earnings growth expectations, limited exposure to AI and elevated energy prices, the report said.Morgan Stanley said the balance of risks remained constructive for now. However, the outlook will depend on whether economic resilience and productivity gains can continue to offset the effects of higher energy prices and inflation.
Article Summary: Strong economic growth, rising corporate earnings and AI-led productivity support returns despite higher bond yields. Oil supply shock that forces central banks to tighten monetary policy excessively is a key risk to its positive outlook for risk assets. US equities preferred, India faces challenges from comparatively weaker forward earnings growth expectations.

Article Title: Trillion dollar gap: US budget deficit swells to nearly $2 tn in fiscal 2026
Article Text:
US annual budget gap touches $2 trillion

Interest burden grows alongside US debt

Supreme Court ruling leads to $145 billion in tariff refunds

The US government spent nearly $2 trillion more than it collected in the 2026 fiscal year, widening its budget deficit to the higest in five years. Higher debt payments, tariff refunds and increased spending on social benefits and defence contributed to the rise.The shortfall increased by $217 billion from the previous year, reaching $1.99 trillion, according to figures released by the treasury department on Friday.The deficit, recorded in the year to September 30, was the largest in five years and the third-largest annual shortfall on record. It was also the first full fiscal year of President Donald Trump's second term. The last time the US recorded a bigger deficit was in fiscal 2021, when the shortfall reached $2.77 trillion amid spending on Covid-19 pandemic relief measures.The latest figures show that although government revenue rose to a record, expenditure grew considerably faster. Receipts increased by $169 billion, or 3%, to $5.40 trillion in fiscal 2026 from $5.24 trillion a year earlier. Outlays, meanwhile, rose by $386 billion, or 6%, to an unprecedented $7.40 trillion, compared with $7.01 trillion in fiscal 2025.The resulting gap was wider than the $1.78 trillion deficit recorded in the previous fiscal year.The cost of servicing the government's debt continued to weigh on public finances, with debt-service expenditure reaching a record $1.36 trillion. The amount was $144 billion, or 12%, higher than in the previous fiscal year.Debt servicing is now the government's third-largest spending category, surpassed only by Social Security and the combined expenditure on Medicare and Medicaid. The increase comes after total US debt crossed $40 trillion about two months ago.Rising expenditure on social benefit programmes, including Social Security and Medicare, also contributed to the higher deficit. Defence spending recorded another substantial increase, rising by 6% to $917 billion during the fiscal year, up $48 billion.A treasury official told Reuters that the department could not determine how much of the increase in defence expenditure was linked to the war Trump and Israel started against Iran earlier this year.The government's tariff collections took a hit after a Supreme Court ruling this year invalidated a large portion of the tariffs imposed by Trump during his first year in office.The ruling led to $145 billion in tariff refunds during fiscal 2026. Net tariff receipts consequently fell by $22 billion, with net tariff income declining 11% to approximately $173 billion. The reduction in collections was another factor behind the widening budget gap.The treasury department estimated the deficit at 6.2% of GDP for fiscal 2026. This was higher than the actual deficit-to-GDP ratio of 5.8% recorded in fiscal 2025. A Treasury official, however, declined to specify the GDP estimate used to calculate the latest ratio.The final month of the fiscal year also ended in deficit. The US government recorded a $27 billion shortfall in September, compared with a surplus of $198 billion in the same month a year earlier.
Article Summary: The shortfall increased by $217 billion from the previous year, reaching $1.99 trillion. The last time the US recorded a bigger deficit was in fiscal 2021, when the shortfall reached $2.77 trillion amid spending on Covid-19 pandemic relief measures.

Article Title: Trump waives Russia sanctions, restrictions and duties under Graham Act
Article Text:
Diesel prices have become a growing political concern ahead of the November 3 midterm elections

US President Donald Trump has waived several sanctions, restrictions and duties targeting Russia under the Graham Act, just weeks after signing the legislation aimed at squeezing Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine. The move comes as his administration seeks to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November’s midterm elections.In an executive order issued on Saturday, Trump invoked a provision of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 that allows the president to waive its measures in the national interest. He said he had submitted the required certification and a report explaining the basis for the decision to Congress.The order waives duties provided for under Sections 112 and 113 of the Act, sanctions and restrictions under Section 102(d), and several other provisions covering sanctions against foreign persons and restrictions on individuals. The waivers will remain in effect until Trump or the secretary of state, in consultation with other officials where appropriate, determines that further action is necessary.The move follows Trump's announcement that the US would purchase Russian diesel after he held what he described as a “highly successful discussion” with Russian President Vladimir Putin.Trump said Moscow had agreed to supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by additional shipments in November and subsequent months.“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump said on Truth Social.The US president added that lowering fuel costs for Americans, particularly farmers, ranchers and truckers, was his “Greatest Priority”.Diesel prices have become a growing political concern ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Prices reached a record $6.52 a gallon in September and were around $6.28 on Friday, putting pressure on businesses and consumers.Under the executive order, the US Trade Representative, in consultation with other senior officials, will monitor countries' purchases of Russian crude oil and natural gas, as well as efforts to evade sanctions, and report developments to the president. The order also provides for additional duties of 500% on Russian goods, subject to specified exceptions and waivers, and 100% on goods from certain major importers of Russian energy and facilitators of sanctions evasion.The shift also comes after Washington repeatedly pressured India to curb its purchases of Russian energy, using tariff threats to push New Delhi to reduce its reliance on Moscow.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has waived several sanctions, restrictions and duties targeting Russia under the Graham Act. The move comes as his administration seeks to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November’s midterm elections. The waivers will remain in effect until Trump or the secretary of state determines that further action is necessary.

Article Title: Wall Street stocks fall as tech selloff weighs on S&P 500, Nasdaq
Article Text:
Technology and chip stocks dragged the Nasdaq down 1.3% and the S&P 500 0.61%

Wall Street's main stock indexes were lower on Friday, as renewed selling in technology and chip stocks weighed on the broader market amid concerns over rising borrowing costs and debt-funded investments in artificial intelligence (AI).The S&P 500 fell 0.61%, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.3%, putting both indexes on track for weekly losses. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was nearly flat, up 0.01%, and headed for a weekly gain, Reuters reported.Technology stocks remained under pressure as investors reassessed the financing behind the AI infrastructure boom. CoreWeave shares fell 9% on Friday and were on track to lose nearly 23% for the week, amid growing scrutiny of the funding required for large-scale AI infrastructure investments."We're starting to see some cracks in the financing of data centers because you're not too sure who's going to be the winners," Tom Plumb, portfolio manager at Plumb Balanced Fund, told Reuters.Concerns over inflation and the prospect of higher interest rates have also unsettled markets. Stronger-than-expected US consumer and wholesale inflation data this week prompted traders to increase bets on further Federal Reserve rate hikes.Meanwhile, US Treasury yields eased on Friday as bond markets stabilised following a rush towards safe-haven assets in the previous session. The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note stood at 5.085%, according to Reuters.Among individual stocks, Micron Technology, Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom and Intel declined, while gains in financial stocks helped limit broader market losses.Elsewhere, Brent crude futures rose 0.85% to $106.83 per barrel, supported by concerns over oil supplies amid heightened tensions in the Middle East and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz.
Article Summary: Nasdaq down 1.3%, S&P 500 0.61%, Dow Jones Industrial Average 0.01%. Concerns over rising borrowing costs and debt-funded investments in AI. Brent crude futures rise 0.85% to $106.83 per barrel, supported by concerns over oil supplies.

Article Title: 1.14 lakh startups generate more than 12 lakh jobs in India: Finance ministry
Article Text:
Finance Ministry

NEW DELHI: More than 1.14 lakh startups in India have created over 12 lakh jobs so far, the finance ministry said in its latest review of the Indian economy.In the report titled, ‘The Indian Economy: A Review January 2024’, the Department of Economic Affairs said that the 1.14 lakh startups recognised by the government under the 'Startup India initiative’ created more than 12 lakh jobs (as of October 2023).The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023, the document read.Despite facing global challenges in 2023 like valuation issues, few IPOs, regulatory changes and macroeconomic and geopolitical trends, India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year.The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion (from 2019 to 2023), according to a recent report by Nasscom in collaboration with Zinnov.“In 2023, despite facing global economic and regulatory challenges, Indian tech startups have prioritised the imperative of enhancing their business fundamentals, driving profitability and growth,” said Debjani Ghosh, President, Nasscom.“The proliferation of tech startups in tier 2 and 3 cities marks the ecosystem's resilience,” she added.Navigating 2024, tech startup founders expect to continue the revenue growth path with measured steps focusing on optimising expenditure and maximising profitability for B2B tech startups.Investments in deeptech will continue an upward trend in 2024. With generative AI (GenAI) acceleration, 70 per cent of start-up founders are embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in their solutions.As funding becomes scarce for the Indian startup ecosystem in general, the explosion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has given a new lease of life to entrepreneurs and founders in the country, as the Centre extends support to the sector.
Article Summary: The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023. India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year. The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion.

Article Title: Startups Revolutionizing Carbon Dioxide into Valuable Products
Article Text: For most perfume makers, ingredients to make it smell great are the most important feature. But for Stafford Sheehan, a cofounder and chemist at Air Company, the most important part of perfume-making has no scent at all.New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. While the pale yellow-color Air Eau de Parfum is about 50% more expensive than Coco Chanel’s signature No. 5, Sheehan says his product is uniquely valuable: Every 50-milliliter bottle uses 3.6 grams of CO2 that otherwise would have been released into the atmosphere. Its package reads: “Turning CO2 into something beautiful.”While the volume of CO2 utilized in the bottle is extremely small, Air Company’s perfume showcases one way the coming wave of captured carbon can be put to use. Renewable energy and electric cars alone won’t be enough to cut CO2 emissions to zero. The world will almost certainly need to capture billions of tons of the gas annually in the coming decades. Large amounts will likely be stored underground.Using it — so-called carbon capture and utilization, or CCU — to create new products from perfume to jet fuel could be an important tool in the fight against climate change, too, though the nascent industry has major hurdles to overcome.Roughly 230 million tons of CO2 are utilized every year, according to a 2019 report by the International Energy Agency. While roughly one-third of that is reused to force more oil from the ground — hardly a carbon-neutral process — CCU advocates say that the number of companies coming up with new uses for carbon has mushroomed in recent years, paving a way to unlock climate benefits. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology and lower costs.Calgary-based CleanO2 transforms CO2 captured from building heating boilers into feedstock to make soap. Newlight Technologies, a biotechnology startup based in California, takes carbon pulled directly from the air and turns it into biodegradable plastics. Germany’s Covestro AG, one of the world’s largest polymer manufacturers, is also switching some of its fossil fuel-based feedstocks to carbon-derived materials for everything ranging from car shells to medical devices and stadium roofs.Most companies working on CO2-sequestering products are still in their infancy. To grow the emerging sector, global venture capitalists in 2022 poured nearly $500 million into carbon utilization businesses, according to the IEA. That’s in stark contrast to 2015, when barely any venture money went to technologies that utilize CO2.“It’s just a whole different landscape today than it was a decade ago,” says Sasha Mackler, executive director of the energy program at Washington, DC-based non-profit Bipartisan Policy Center.Jennifer Holmgren, chief executive officer of LanzaTech Global Inc., has experienced the shifting sentiment firsthand. The Illinois-based company uses a carbon-eating bacteria – discovered in the guts of rabbits and preserved as powder – to make alternative ethanol in bioreactors not dissimilar to how breweries ferment beer. In the early 2010s, when Holmgren touted carbon-derived ethanol to prospective customers, her sales pitch was met with skepticism.But the tide began turning later that decade. In 2018, the company’s jet fuel produced from the emissions of a Chinese steel mill helped power a Transatlantic flight. LanzaTech has also inked agreements with airlines including Japan’s All Nippon Airways to supply CO2-derived jet fuel. And LanzaJet, the company’s spin-off, plans to start producing sustainable jet fuels at a commercial scale this year.Yet for all the hype around sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) using captured carbon, the industry is still an extremely small player. Almost every major airline in the world has pledged to use at least 10% sustainable jet fuels by 2030, yet SAF makes up only 0.1% of global aviation fuel supply — and much of it is made from sources other than captured CO2, such as used cooking oil.“There’s a lot more interest because consumers have become much more interested in buying things that are lower carbon,” says Holmgren. That’s enabled LanzaTech to expand the number of products that utilize CO2.American plastic container maker Plastipak, for instance, has partnered with LanzaTech to produce carbon-derived packaging materials, while polyester converted from LanzaTech’s ethanol has replaced its petroleum-based counterpart at a pilot scale in Lululemon shorts, Zara dresses, H&M yoga pants, On running shoes and Craghoppers jackets. Like SAF, though, there’s still a long way to go for CO2-derived polyester to reach meaningful levels of use.Momentum to grow beyond one-off products and low-scale production has also been supercharged by a growing array of regulations and incentives around the world. For instance, the Inflation Reduction Act that US President Joe Biden signed in 2022 raised the tax credit for carbon capture and utilization by more than 70% to $60 per metric ton in an effort to make costly projects more financially appealing.To keep the climate within habitable limits, the IEA estimates that carbon capture will have to grow to 7.6 billion tons of CO2 annually by mid-century. CCU will play a role, though just how big remains to be seen. Not every use case is created equal and some approaches, such as dissolving compressed CO2 in water to make carbonated beverages, only store the gas temporarily. To quantify the true climate benefit of carbon utilization, experts say third-party verification is badly needed.The rise of CCU technology comes as another key approach in President Biden’s net-zero roadmap is hitting a bit of a wall. Carbon capture and storage — that is, gathering CO2 as it’s released from a coal-fired power plant or other emissions source and sequestering it underground — has faced challenges because carbon is often captured in one place and stored in another. That requires pipelines to transport the gas, which many local communities have opposed. Blackrock-backed Navigator, for example, recently announced it was scrapping a planned 1,300-mile CO2 pipeline.Carbon utilization companies say that they can sidestep that issue by using carbon near or at where it’s captured.At its 12-acre factory in Brooklyn, Glenwood Mason Supply demonstrates how. The concrete manufacturer takes CO2 captured at a residential building by its partner company, CarbonQuest, and uses a technique licensed from low-carbon concrete startup CarbonCure to convert the compressed carbon into a powder not unlike dry ice. It then injects it into industrial mixers. There, the CO2 meets cement, sand and aggregate, setting off a series of chemical reactions. The final result is concrete blocks with CO2 sealed in.The technique not only stores carbon but it can also make the blocks marginally stronger. The company estimates that it has utilized about 100 tons of CO2 in total since 2020. Even if the blocks break down, the stored carbon won’t be released as CO2 because it’s been mineralized.“Cement is a big offender in carbon emissions,” says Constance Cincotta, founder of the concrete factory. She became intrigued by the technology and its ability to lower her company's climate impact after hearing about it at an industry conference in the early 2010s. But it wasn't until CarbonCure came on the scene a few years ago that the prospect of CO2-storing cement became tangible. Glenwood Mason then sourced CO2 locally from CarbonQuest, which captures carbon from buildings in New York. Those factors have enabled large-scale production.While Cincotta’s intended to help the planet, she and her team discovered that sinking CO2 into concrete blocks is good for the business, too. In 2019, New York City — where the majority of the company’s concrete blocks are sold — passed a regulation requiring all buildings to shrink their carbon footprint 40% by the end of the decade. Glenwood Mason’s phones have been ringing ever since, with calls from architects and property developers who want to leverage their lower-carbon building materials to cut emissions, says Jeff Hansen, the company’s vice president in architectural sales and marketing.The factory’s CO2-storing concrete blocks also caught the eye of Amazon.com Inc, which in 2022 persuaded a real estate developer to purchase roughly 50,000 blocks for the construction of a new warehouse in New York that Amazon has leased. Had Glenwood Mason not sealed CO2 in its blocks, it wouldn’t have won the contract, Hansen says. To figure out how to pack more carbon into its products, the company has set up a laboratory in its factory to test the reaction between CO2 and other concrete feedstocks under different temperatures and humidity levels.But figuring out the right formula is only one consideration. Utilizing CO2 often comes with an additional cost. As the demand for CO2-derived products climbs, that green premium is expected to go down. Yet “it’s very hard to be a cost parity with a 100-year-old industry that doesn’t even have to pay for its externalities,” says Holmgren of LanzaTech. Even with economies of scale, Holmgren estimates that carbon-containing fabrics will still likely cost as much as 20% higher than conventional ones.“It’s unlikely that we will ever be a cost parity,” she says.In addition to the cost barrier, CCU companies also have to convince end users that may be suspicious of unproven new technologies.Changing feedstocks “does come with risks,” says Keith Wiggins, chief executive officer of Econic Technologies, a British startup that specializes in making carbon-derived chemicals. To get risk-averse industries onboard, Wiggins says his company is laser-focused on those that are under consumer pressure to change course.That strategy seems to be working. Econic has teamed up with three manufacturers in the US, China and India to produce mattresses, outdoor garments and building insulation materials that utilize CO2. The first batch of products using the company’s technology are scheduled to enter the market in 2024.For all the promise of the carbon utilization industry, it remains to be seen if it can challenge the status quo. While Air Company started selling carbon-derived perfume in 2021, the startup has yet to build its first commercial plant, Sheehan says, citing the time-consuming process needed for collecting data and fine-tuning the technology for large-scale production.Fow now, the company’s demonstration facility in New York City — where CO2 and hydrogen gas flow through tubes into a reactor to form chemical reactions, aided by catalysts made from a confidential mixture of metals — is designed to yield at least 10,000 gallons of CO2-derived liquid annually. The limited production capacity has left many orders for its perfume — as well as jet fuels and Air Vodka, another popular product made from CO2 — unfilled.“We need to scale these facilities to the size of oil refineries today in order to have the impact on climate change that we want to have,” Sheehan says.
Article Summary: New York-based Air Company uses technology that converts planet-warming carbon dioxide into ethanol, which is then blended with essential oils and water to produce perfume. Carbon-derived fuels and chemicals, for example, could theoretically grow to the scale of billions of tons of CO2 use per year if companies could perfect their technology.

Article Title: E-commerce firm Udaan raises $340 million ahead of planned IPO
Article Text: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain and boost vendor partnerships ahead of a stock market debut planned for 2025.The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt, the Bangalore-based company said in a statement Thursday. The round was led by M&G Plc and existing investors including Lightspeed Venture Partners and DST Global participated.The round “fully funds our business plan,” Vaibhav Gupta, Udaan co-founder and chief executive officer, said in the statement. “It enables our continued journey of growth and profitability, positioning us well to be public-market ready in the next 12-18 months.”Udaan, which competes with Reliance Industries Ltd. and Walmart Inc.’s Flipkart in helping smaller merchants source their goods, runs an online marketplace and logistics networks that help mum-and-pop stores get quicker deliveries and cut traditional middlemen out. That kind of digital-led wholesale business, though a very small part of India’s overall retail market, is expected to swell to $150 billion in sales in a decade, according to McKinsey & Co.The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas, Gupta told Bloomberg News last month.Udaan was founded in 2016 by three engineers who previously worked at Flipkart. The trio together ran the company until Gupta, one of the founders, took over as CEO in 2021. The other two founders — Amod Malviya and Sujeet Kumar — are board members.
Article Summary: Indian e-commerce firm Udaan raised $340 million to strengthen its supply chain. The Series E round was done via a combination of fresh equity and conversion of debt. The startup targets an initial public offering in 2025, though it’s yet to decide whether it will do so in India or overseas.

Article Title: Minuscule AI startup raises $41 million to tap India growth
Article Text: A generative artificial intelligence startup targeting the Indian market raised $41 million in fresh funding, the largest such round by an early-stage AI contender in the country.Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages at price points that the country’s 1.4 billion people can afford. The Series A funding round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, and participants included Silicon Valley billionaire Vinod Khosla’s Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners, formerly Sequoia Capital India & Southeast Asia, Sarvam said Thursday.The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co-founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems as well as tools for creating apps for the meager compute infrastructure available to developers in India. The startup has a total of 18 employees and is just opening an office in the city."What we are showing is that you can build large language models with limited resources,” Raghavan said in a phone interview. "We are building at a smaller scale and demonstrating that these can be extremely cost and energy efficient so they can be accessed by everyone."Large language models, like OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama, are powerful AI systems that understand by learning from vast amounts of diverse data from the internet and elsewhere to summarize, translate, and create text, audio and video for a wide range of applications. The rivalry to develop ever-more sophisticated models is heating up in Silicon Valley and such efforts have attracted billions of dollars in investments.
Article Summary: Sarvam AI is building large language models targeted at unique uses in Indian languages. The Bangalore-based startup, until recently in stealth mode, was co- founded by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar. It has ambitious plans to build open source foundational AI systems.

Article Title: ZestMoney set to shut operations this month
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Buy now Pay Later (BNPL) startup ZestMoney has decided to shut operations. The move will impact some 150 employees of the firm, the company's management told employees in a town hall on Tuesday. ZestMoney did not comment. It is learnt that the firm will shut down by the end of this month.The move comes after attempts by the Bengaluru-based startup to get acquired by larger peer PhonePe failed. The deal was called off earlier this year after a due diligence process undertaken by PhonePe, while evaluating the potential acquisition failed to meet its bar. The Walmart-owned fintech major had, however, hired some 130 of ZestMoney's employees.
Article Summary: The move will impact some 150 employees of the firm, the company's management told employees in a town hall on Tuesday. The move comes after attempts by the Bengaluru-based startup to get acquired by larger peer PhonePe failed. The Walmart-owned fintech major had, however, hired some 130 of ZestMoney's employees.

Article Title: Startups will play important role in helping India become 3rd largest economy: CEA Nageswaran
Article Text:
Chief Economic Advisor V Anantha Nageswaran





THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: Startups will play an important role in helping India become the third largest economy in the world, Chief Economic Advisor (CEA) to the Union government V Anantha Nageswaran has said.Nageswaran said that tier-2 and 3 cities, including Kerala's capital, have become game-changers in helping startups flourish in the country due to improvements in infrastructure and supportive policies of the government, according to a KSUM release.The CEA, during his Leadership Talk on the concluding day of the Huddle Global 2023 organised by the Kerala Startup Mission (KSUM), said that India was the fifth largest economy on course to become the third largest in a few years."In fact, I will say 7-in-7 is the buzz slogan, that is 7 trillion USD economy in seven years. Seven trillion USD economy size by 2030 is possible if India maintains its present growth trajectory, and in that journey startup entrepreneurs are going to play an important role," he is quoted as having said in the release.He was of the view that the active participation of startups in India in developing business models on the foundation of expanding physical and digital infrastructure will continue to generate efficiency, revenue and economic returns for the country."The last decade has seen an exceptional transformation in the startup landscape in India, which has emerged as the third largest ecosystem globally, with over 1.12 lakh startups presently recognised by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) across 763 districts."Among them, more than 110 are unicorns with a total valuation of around USD 350 billion," he said.The CEA further said that the country ranks second in innovation quality.He said that innovation in India was not just limited to certain sectors as startups were solving problems in 56 industrial sectors, with 13 per cent of them from IT services, nine per cent from health and life sciences, seven per cent from education, five per cent from agriculture and five per cent from food and beverages.Nageswaran also said it was significant that 49 per cent of the startups were from tier-2 and 3 cities which have turned to be game-changers as the business advantages in these locations enable entrepreneurs to operate at lower costs as compared to tier-1 cities."Apart from improved infrastructure and the government's pro-active policies, the availability of a technically skilled talent pool is a huge advantage for startups to set up and flourish in tier-2 and tier-3 cities," he said.He said that historically there was a perception that small towns were difficult places to conduct business."...but with improved internet penetration, vastly better physical infrastructure, road, rail and air connectivity and supportive government policies, this is no longer true," he said.He also noted Kerala's startup journey has been an inspiring one.The CEA said that KSUM has served as the catalyst since its establishment in 2006 to promote change that propelled the state into the forefront of the global startup arena.KSUM is the Kerala government's nodal agency established in 2006 for entrepreneurship development and incubation activities in the state.Nageswaran said that with over 4,000 registered tech startups, 63 incubators and 10 lakh square feet of incubation space, KSUM has not only met its goal of promoting technology-based entrepreneurship but has also earned the distinguished position of being among the world's top business incubators.The November 16-18 fifth edition of Huddle Global, India's biggest beachside startup conclave, was organised by KSUM at Adimalathura beach, near Vizhinjam, here.Attended by around 1,500 delegates, the event displayed sophisticated products from emerging sectors such as robotics, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Augmented Reality, Virtual Reality, life sciences, space tech, blockchain, IoT, e-governance, fintech, healthtech, agritech, edutech and SaaS from across the country.
Article Summary: Chief Economic Advisor V Anantha Nageswaran said tier-2 and 3 cities, including Kerala's capital, have become game-changers in helping startups flourish in the country. CEA said that India was the fifth largest economy on course to become the third largest in a few years.

Article Title: E-Commerce startup Udaan to trim costs ahead of 2025 IPO
Article Text: E-commerce startup Udaan is working to curb costs and forge new partnerships with consumer brands in India as it prepares to go public in 2025.Udaan, which competes with Reliance Industries Ltd. and Walmart Inc.’s Flipkart in helping smaller merchants source their goods, will make an operating profit within 18 months, Chief Executive Officer Vaibhav Gupta said in an interview. That’s set to happen around the same time as its initial public offering, he said.The priority “is steady and predictable financial performance,” Gupta said. “Second, strategically we want to ensure that we are top of mind with shopkeepers, with big manufacturers, and we maintain our relative market share.”Lightspeed Venture Partners-backed Udaan is among startups trying to tap the rapid growth of India’s economy and consumer market, while meeting investor demands for profitability. Udaan, which at its peak employed thousands, joined fellow Indian startups in slashing jobs last year and tightening internal controls and compliance. It now has about 1,800 staff, and Gupta didn’t specify if further job cuts are needed.Corporate governance lapses at Indian online tutoring firm Byju’s, once the country’s top startup with a valuation of $22 billion, shone a light at unique challenges faced by founders in the South Asian nation and drove companies to be more diligent.“We continue to move towards more professionalized management, professionalized board and also institutionalized shareholders as we go towards public markets,” Gupta said.Udaan is yet to decide whether it will list in India or overseas. It was valued at more than $3 billion in a 2021 funding round, and was in talks to raise $400 million, Business Standard reported in September. Lightspeed owns about 35% of Udaan, while Tencent Holdings Ltd. holds 6%.The company was founded in 2016 by three engineers who previously worked at Flipkart. The trio together ran Udaan until Gupta, one of the founders, took over as CEO in 2021. The other two founders — Amod Malviya and Sujeet Kumar — are board members.Udaan built an online marketplace and logistics networks that help mum-and-pop stores get quicker deliveries and cut traditional middlemen out. That kind of digital-led wholesale business still accounts for a very small part of India’s overall retail market but can balloon to $150 billion in sales and yield a 100% return on capital invested in a decade, according to McKinsey & Co. estimates published in the Mint newspaper.Bengaluru-based Udaan has also ventured into financing through its fintech unit which helps shopkeepers get working capital loans to buy inventory. That business is profitable before taxes and is growing 70% annually, Gupta said.“That’s a second business in the overall umbrella of Udaan trying to organize trade in the country,” Gupta said. “In addition to commerce, financing becomes an important market opportunity.”
Article Summary: Udaan will make an operating profit within 18 months, Chief Executive Officer Vaibhav Gupta says. Udaan competes with Reliance Industries Ltd. and Walmart Inc.’s Flipkart in helping smaller merchants source their goods. The priority “is steady and predictable financial performance,” Gupta said.

Article Title: Kerala-based startup bags prestigious awards
Article Text: KOCHI: A company under the Kerala Startup Mission (KSUM), which primarily connects devotees with temples through a cost-free Customer Relationship Management Solution (CRM), has bagged two prestigious awards in a week's time, boosting its profile fuelled by three years of ground-breaking ‘BookSeva'.InIT Solutions Pvt Ltd was honoured with the ‘ Emerging Startup of the Year 2023 Award ', followed by another at the Entrepreneurship Conclave 2023 (EC2023) earlier this month, a press release said here on Saturday.The 2011-founded InIT, whose CRM solution is tailored specifically for temple administration, won the first of the two honours on September 30 at the HSX2.0 event hosted by Headstart at SAP Labs Bangalore, it said.The second came at the October 7-8 EC2023 organised by the World Konkani Centre, Saraswath Chamber and UK & Co, it said.InIT won the ‘Emerging Startup' recognition at a competition between 1,000 startups from across the country.The company emerged in the standout selections among the 70 startups shortlisted, earning it the spotlight at the Bharath Pitchathon 2.0, it said.As for the EC2023 honour, the event recognised InIT Solutions Pvt Ltd as one of the ‘Top 5 Startups' that had excelled in the SharkTank Pitching competition.The event was held before experts such as Infosys former director Mohandas Pai and Jyothi Labs ex-CEO Ullas Kamath besides 300-plus visionary entrepreneurs, investors and corporate representatives from across India.Each of these top startups, including InIT, won a prize of Rs 5 lakh, the statement further said.Besides ‘BookSeva', InIT assists temples in streamlining their day-to-day operations by implementing an ERP (enterprise resource planning) system.Notable Kerala temple administrations associating with InIT are Guruvayur, those under Cochin Devaswom Board and Attukal in Thiruvananthapuram district.InIT Solutions, which is based at Vennala in the city, is working towards expanding its services to temple management across India, it added.KSUM is Kerala government's nodal agency established in 2006 for entrepreneurship development and incubation activities.
Article Summary: InIT Solutions Pvt Ltd was honoured with the ‘ Emerging Startup of the Year 2023 Award' The company primarily connects devotees with temples through a cost-free Customer Relationship Management Solution (CRM) The 2011-founded InIT, whose CRM solution is tailored specifically for temple administration, won the first of the two honours.

Article Title: Startup BharatAgri raises Rs 35 crore from investors
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Agritech startup BharatAgri, an advisory led e-commerce platform for farmers, on Thursday said it has raised Rs 35 crore (USD 4.3 million) from investors including Arkam Ventures.The company raised Rs 35 crore in the Series A funding round.Besides Arkam Ventures the funding round also saw participation from Capria Ventures and existing investors, India Quotient, 021 Capital , and Omnivore , BharatAgri said in a release.The funding marks Arkam Ventures' third investment in the agri-tech space."The funds will be used to scale BharatAgri's e-commerce platform into new geographies and strengthen its last-mile delivery," the statement said.BharatAgri, founded by IIT Madras Alumni Siddharth Dialani and Sai Gole, has built prediction algorithms that provide advisory customised to crops, region and climatic changes.Farmers can access this custom advisory that would help them increase farm yield, lower input costs and labour effort.Its e-commerce platform offers over 10,000 agricultural products such as fertilisers, seeds, pesticides, insecticides, farming equipment, among others and is delivered pan-India, the statement said.
Article Summary: Agritech startup BharatAgri, an advisory led e-commerce platform for farmers, on Thursday said it has raised Rs 35 crore (USD 4.3 million) from investors including Arkam Ventures. The company raised Rs35 crore in the Series A funding round. The funding round also saw participation from Capria Ventures and existing investors, India Quotient, 021 Capital, and Omnivore.

Article Title: Medicine: Co-living startup Settl to enter Chennai market, to add 1,000 beds by March for working professionals
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Co-living startup Settl on Thursday said it will foray into the Chennai market and launch 300 beds soon for working professionals.Bengaluru-based Settl is currently managing 3,500 beds across Bengaluru, Gurugram and Hyderabad. It has 1,200 beds in Gurugram, 1,700 beds in Bengaluru, and 600 beds in Hyderabad.It offers rental accommodation between Rs 11,000 to Rs 24,000 per month per bed, depending on the location, city and available amenities."We are looking to expand our business as demand for quality rental accommodations which are fully managed, is rising. Chennai offers a huge potential for co-living centres. We have identified a few buildings and are in talks with landlords to onboard these properties," Settl Co-Founder Abhishek Tripathi said in a statement.To begin with, the company plans to launch 300 beds in Chennai and will scale up to 1,000 beds by the end of this fiscal.Established in 2020, Settl enters into long-term lease agreements with builders and asset owners. It designs and develops the properties before sub-leasing the space to working professionals.
Article Summary: Bengaluru-based Settl is currently managing 3,500 beds across Bengaluru, Gurugram and Hyderabad. The company plans to launch 300 beds in Chennai and will scale up to 1,000 beds by the end of this fiscal.
